name: Distributed Ledger
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: One Ledger, No Single Keeper
lesson.summary: A distributed ledger is a record of transactions that many independent computers hold and update together, so no single party controls the official copy.
lesson.body:
Every ledger, whether it is a medieval merchant's account book or a modern bank's database, exists to answer one question: who owns what, and what changed hands. For most of history the answer to "who keeps the official copy" was simple: one institution did, and everyone else trusted it. A distributed ledger changes that answer. Instead of one custodian holding the single authoritative record, many independent computers, called nodes, each hold a full or partial copy of the same record and update it in step with one another.

This idea rests on two things covered earlier in this course: distributed systems and data integrity. A distributed system is simply a collection of computers that work together and communicate over a network to accomplish a shared task, without any one machine being in charge of the others. A distributed ledger applies that architecture to record-keeping specifically. Data integrity, meanwhile, is what makes the arrangement trustworthy rather than chaotic: each node's copy must be verifiably the same as every other node's copy, and any tampering with one copy must be detectable by comparing it against the rest.

Consider three roommates who split rent and shared expenses over a year. If only one roommate keeps the spreadsheet, the other two must simply trust her arithmetic and her honesty. If instead all three keep their own copy of the same running list, and they compare notes regularly, an error or a dishonest edit by one person becomes visible the moment the copies are checked against each other. That comparison is crude compared to what a real distributed ledger does with cryptography, but the underlying logic is identical: redundancy plus comparison produces trust that no single copy could provide on its own.

The practical benefit is resilience. A centralized ledger has a single point of failure: if the custodian's server crashes, gets hacked, or the institution itself becomes corrupt or coerced, the record is compromised or lost. A distributed ledger spreads that risk across many independent participants, so no single failure destroys the record and no single party can quietly rewrite history without the rewrite standing out against everyone else's copy.

It is worth being skeptical about what "distributed" buys you, though. Distribution is not free. Keeping many copies synchronized takes network bandwidth, storage, and a way for nodes to agree when their copies briefly disagree, which is a genuinely hard problem addressed by ledger replication, covered next. And distributed ledgers are a broader category than blockchains: some distributed ledgers use very different data structures than the chained blocks this course will get to shortly. Calling something "distributed" describes who holds the data, not how well the system performs or how decentralized its governance actually is in practice.
